pr_title: Do not fail if ctx dup does not succeed
pr_body:
If the ctx was *really* needed we'll probably fail later with an error anyway, so no point in failing immediately.

In most cases users will actually not follow-up with additional requests, so by failing later we will allow more use cases when a provider can't support duplication.

Fixes #20364 

<!-- Remove items that do not apply. For completed items, change [ ] to [x]. -->
- [ ] documentation is added or updated
- [ ] tests are added or updated
pr_comments:
Shouldn't we also be doing the same change in `EVP_DigestVerifyFinal`?

`EVP_SignFinal` and `EVP_VerifyFinal` also duplicate the `EVP_MD_CTX` - although maybe that is less of an issue.

Can you also update the man pages? In particular this section needs update:

```` text
The call to EVP_DigestSignFinal() internally finalizes a copy of the digest
context. This means that calls to EVP_DigestSignUpdate() and
EVP_DigestSignFinal() can be called later to digest and sign additional data.
````

@mattcaswell if you confirm this way of solving the issue is acceptable, I will fix all context dups to be have the same way across the codebase, and add doc changes to reflect it.

Do you confirm this is just legacy behavior and no code (like in the TLS code paths) depend on this context duplication behavior?

@mattcaswell btw I updated the PR to deal with EVP_DigestVerifyFinal and add the note in the docs about not all providers necessarily supporting that and what happens if not.

As I was looking at the code while doing this I realize EVP_DigestSign and EVP_DigestVerify have a fallback case where they will attempt to call the ..Update/..Final calls, technically if they fallback they will end up not finalising the md context.

This looks underspecified in the docs. My reading is the docs assume EVP_DigestSign/Verify always finialise the context.

Given it is just a fallback case, and the common case will not allow for continuation, should I add a patch to set the EVP_MD_CTX_FLAG_FINALISE before falling back so that no unnecessary context duplication is done and there is no continuation case?
Would it be possible to have a test for this?
In theory yes, the provider that provides a digest and fails the context duplication should do the trick

> Would it be possible to have a test for this?

I will try to add one next, still need to check EVP_Sign/VerifyFinal which I think I missed, I looked only at the Digest ones right now.
@t8m I added a test
@simo5 the failures look relevant

@beldmit I do not see any failures ...
@mattcaswell fixing
@beldmit sorry, apparently my browser had not updated the page consistently, I see a few failing tests now
@beldmit the errors seem to be leaks, I should have all fixed in my next push
CI still failing
Looks like it is still memleaks ... I will dig deeper.

> If the ctx was *really* needed we'll probably fail later with an error anyway, so no point in failing immediately.

This sounds to me like a recipe for cryptographic failure where you're not sure what you actually did.

> If the ctx was *really* needed we'll probably fail later with an error anyway, so no point in failing immediately.
> This sounds to me like a recipe for cryptographic failure where you're not sure what you actually did.

I am not sure what you are talking about here, care to explain?
Keep in mind that not a single test is failing in OpenSSL because of this change. This is an ancient, untested, behavior that probably no software relies on.

If we could break promises I would favor completely removing the behavior altogether TBH.

It is just not a good practice, and it is probably not used, therefore just additional complexity to keep around for no good reason.
@t8m looks like all tests are passing now
@beldmit can you please reconfirm your approval?
I reconfirm. I don't know what can be done to test it to a deeper extent.

My understanding is that you rely on 1 party to correctly implement it, so that if the other is doing something that is broken it will be detected. This sounds like a very bad idea. The **probably** in your sentence is really worrisome. But maybe I'm misunderstanding things.

It's not because we currently have no tests that cover this, that nobody is using this.

> My understanding is that you rely on 1 party to correctly implement it, so that if the other is doing something that is broken it will be detected. This sounds like a very bad idea. The **probably** in your sentence is really worrisome. But maybe I'm misunderstanding things.

I do not understand what "other" party would be involved here.

There is only one program calling EVP_DigestSignUpdate/EVP_DigestSignFinal multiple times.

With the default provider there is no change here.

With a provider that can't support context duplication:
- The first attempt will succeed, and a signature will be correctly generated.
- The second attempt will fail and no signature will be generated.

Note that no code in OpenSSL ever does a second attempt.
I am aware of no code that does it, in fact.

> It's not because we currently have no tests that cover this, that nobody is using this.

Sure, but there are providers that simply can't support this, yet I simply can't fail this for *all* users.
I want to fail this only for those crazy rare users that will attempt a second update+signature on the same context.
@kroeckx hold does not remove the approvals. It just blocks merging.

> The second attempt will fail and no signature will be generated.

Note that this does rely on any provider correctly identifying that it has been incorrectly called. Should it be the EVP layer that somehow detects that update has been called after final?

> > The second attempt will fail and no signature will be generated.
> 
> Note that this does rely on any provider correctly identifying that it has been incorrectly called. Should it be the EVP layer that somehow detects that update has been called after final?

That's a good point. Otherwise we risk silently generating incorrect signatures.

> Note that this does rely on any provider correctly identifying that it has been incorrectly called. Should it be the EVP layer that somehow detects that update has been called after final?

Note that if the application passes the EVP_MD_CTX_FLAG_FINALISE flag this is already the case. I do not see why this would be a problem.

If it is a problem then it is a pre-existing one.

@kroeckx As far as I understand, the code will work as it worked now for the default provider and fips provider. For 3rd-party HW-backed provider this code doesn't work now but should start work in many scenarios. 

The only openssl code that may be affected is TLS in case HMAC is used as EVP_Sign, but I think it's not the case.

> If it is a problem then it is a pre-existing one.

It is a pre-existing problem, however this patch potentially makes it more dangerous because with it it could happen implicitly without setting any extra flag. So, in the end, it would be better to somehow ensure further operations with the context will fail on the evp layer.

@t8m we could free and NULL pctx, however, if we do that, a followup call would hit the legacy path.

One option is to add a new context flag to mark the context finalized, the other is to add an int to the EVP_MD_CTX structure to signify the same.

> @t8m we could free and NULL pctx, however, if we do that, a followup call would hit the legacy path.
> 
> One option is to add a new context flag to mark the context finalized, the other is to add an int to the EVP_MD_CTX structure to signify the same.

I would add the flag on the EVP_MD_CTX.
Working on adding a new flag and setting/checking for it.

@t8m I pushed a tentative commit.
This commit causes failures in some EVP tests, because the tests try to call EVP_DIgestSignFinal with a known short buffer, and expect to be able to call again with the correct inputs and succeed.
But now my patch unconditionally mark the context as finalised therefore the second test always fails.

I see 2 options:
1. Finalise the context only if the underlying calls succeed.
2. Change the tests to reset the context and retry the whole operation.

With (1) no tests have to change. However it is dubious that you should be able to call again after a failure, given we do not know what the nature of the failure is.
OTOH, if there is code out there that rely on similar behavior it would keep working. 

Implementing (2) just means some more churn in the EVP tests, but potential incompatibilities for some odd application.

Ignore (mostly) the previous comment.
I think most of the errors turned out to be an issue I introduced with not checking for sigret == NULL in the Sign/SignFinal calls, that is fixed, we'll see if there are more cases that fail now
@t8m: The reason for removing the approved label had to do with changes I wanted to see. But I might not have been clear enough about that.
With the current patch, I see no security issue any more, and so I've removed the hold label.
This looks good to me. I'm ready to approve subject to the comments from @t8m and @kroeckx being resolved.
@mattcaswell if the manpages language is accepted I think I have provided all the requested changes
Looks like one of the windows checks may have had an infrastructure issue, as there are no results whatsoever. It is the only failure.
This pull request is ready to merge
Merged, thanks.

issue_context.title: Context duplication is often unsupportable with hardware tokens
issue_context.body:
OpenSSL 3.0 default behavior for some operations, like signatures, is to duplicate the operation context, then proceed to complete the signature operation on the duplicated context or fail if the duplication fails.

In the pkcs11-provider I work around this behavior by effectively transferring the context to the duplicate and simply rendering the original context unusable.

This is not ideal, and I would like to raise this as an API problem.

Ideally OpenSSL would *try* to make a duplicate, and on failure continue the operation on the original context but not fail the whole operation.

I can easily send a patch to do that in places like this:
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c1ec72a7abb29f2d91eda6f93942670f1cbdb9e/crypto/evp/m_sigver.c#LL477

However I guess there is a reason why OpenSSL does something as odd as this by default?
My guess is it has to do with some space optimization for TLS handshakes, but I do not know for sure.

I know not all operations depend on context duplication to be completed successfully, because my workaround does work with all command line operations so far (but I do not have TLS tests yet).

This is something of a big deal for any provider that want to expose hardware (or remote) crypto engines, like TPM, HSMs, Smartcards, etc... and natively implement digest/sign APIs.

One option is to revert to software digesting + only raw signatures at the end, but that is not ideal and not all hw will necessarily offer raw signature APIs.

Plus FIPS compliance requires digesting to be done on the token, so it would break that part for users that want to be compliant.

One compromise could be to advertise at context creation time the need to have a duplicate later on, or perhaps the other way around, query some new context param to check if it supports context duplication for the specific algorithm selected ?

If the provider knows in advance that context duplication will be requested, it could change behavior only in those cases if it knows the HW context can't be duplicated.
Otherwise if OpenSSL queries the HW it could decide to take fallback paths, unclear to me what would be the best way.

I am seeking guidance here, and am willing to provide patches.
comments:
Interesting. I was not aware of this "feature".

> However I guess there is a reason why OpenSSL does something as odd as this by default?
My guess is it has to do with some space optimization for TLS handshakes, but I do not know for sure.

No, the reasons behind it are documented in the man page:

> The call to EVP_DigestSignFinal() internally finalizes a copy of the digest
context. This means that calls to EVP_DigestSignUpdate() and
EVP_DigestSignFinal() can be called later to digest and sign additional data.

It seems this behaviour has been there since forever (at lest it exists for EVP_SignFinal in 0.9.8 which is as far back as I checked). At some point there was an attempt to add an option to disable it:

> =item EVP_MD_CTX_FLAG_FINALISE
> 
> Some functions such as EVP_DigestSign only finalise copies of internal
contexts so additional data can be included after the finalisation call.
This is inefficient if this functionality is not required, and can be
disabled with this flag.

But this is a non-default option, and requires the caller to explicitly set it which, I guess, hardly anyone does.

It doesn't seem unreasonable to me to fall back to not duplicating the context if the duplication operation fails. This wouldn't exactly be a compatibility break because, presumably, applications that rely on this are already using providers that support it.

It would have to be a documented restriction of any provider that it doesn't support this "continue signing more data" capability which may make it incompatible with some applications that use this. Probably this couldn't be classed as a "bug fix" though, so master only. We'd also have to update the man pages for the various sign/verfiy functions to explain that some providers may not support this. Perhaps there needs to be some param/API you can query to find out if it is supported or not?
I'd consider this behavior change to 3.1.

EVP_PKEY_CTX_dup seems to be relatively new - AFAIR, EVP_PKEY_CTX appeared in 1.0 series together with pluggable asymmetric algorithms. The problem I see here is that even when digest context is usually more easily duplicated than the EVP_PKEY context...

> Perhaps there needs to be some param/API you can query to find out if it is supported or not?

Yes, I poporsed this above, if you can tell me what to do here, I can implement it in the pkcs11-provider and document.
Meanwhile I am going to propose a code fix and will follow up with a path for docs if we agree the fix is sound.
Do we have anything to do here?
The main PR was done, I think we can close if no more needs to be added.
